questions.stem:
Expedite, Hasten, Hurry, __________

Fill the blank by choosing a word with a meaning similar to that of the words given above.

steps.title: What a synonym question asks
steps.body: Synonyms are words that carry the same core meaning. When a question lists several words, find the one idea they all share, state it in your own words, and pick the option that expresses that same idea. Meaning decides the answer; spelling and sound do not.

steps.title: Find the shared idea
steps.body: To expedite is to make a process finish sooner. To hasten is to cause something to happen sooner. To hurry is to move or act faster. All three mean "make something go faster", and all three are actions you perform to increase speed.

steps.title: Test each option against that idea
steps.body: Accelerate means to increase speed, which is exactly the shared idea. Retard means to slow down, the opposite. Provide means to supply something and has nothing to do with speed. Disable means to put out of working order, which stops a process instead of speeding it.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The word that completes the list is Accelerate, option (A).

shortcut.body: State the common meaning in three words ("make it faster"), then strike any option that is the opposite or unrelated. Only Accelerate survives. Under 30 seconds. Unsafe only when two options both fit, which does not happen here.

traps.text: Retard sits at the opposite pole of the same scale (speed). A hurried reader who notices "speed" and does not check the direction picks it.
Provide sounds like a business verb that goes with expedite (to expedite an order), but it means to supply, not to speed.
Disable looks like a verb in the same register as the others, but it describes stopping a thing from working.

recognize.clues: Three listed words and one blank, with a request for a word of similar meaning. The shared sense of the list is making something happen sooner.
recognize.contrast: An antonym question asks for the opposite. The instruction here says similar, so an option that reverses the direction is a lure, not a match.

check.body: Use a second route: put each word after the same noun. 'Expedite the order', 'hasten the order' and 'hurry the order' all speed it up, and exactly one option reads the same way. The others either reverse the sense or make no sense with a process.

hints.text: What single idea do the three listed words share? Ask what happens to a process when you expedite, hasten or hurry it.
Synonyms match in core meaning, so put that shared meaning into a few plain words before you read the options.
A word that points the opposite way on the same scale is an antonym, and a word about another topic is a distractor. Only a word moving in the same direction qualifies.
Test each option with one question: does this word describe making something go faster? Mark each one as same direction, opposite, or unrelated.
One option names slowing things down and another has nothing to do with speed, so both can be struck before you compare the rest.

variation.stem:
Mend, Repair, Fix, __________

Fill the blank by choosing a word with a meaning similar to that of the words given above.
variation.explanation: The three listed words mean to put something back in working order. Restore carries that meaning. Shatter is the opposite, Inspect is only a step before repair and does not fix anything, and Purchase is about buying.

questions.stem: The antonym of the word protagonist is ________.

steps.title: What an antonym is
steps.body: Antonyms are words whose meanings are opposite on the same scale. Before choosing, say what the given word means, then ask which option stands against it. Look for a role or quality that the two words share and that they hold in opposite directions.

steps.title: Break the word into roots
steps.body: Protagonist comes from Greek protos (first) and agonistes (a contestant in a struggle): the leading character, the one the story follows and who drives the struggle. Antagonist uses anti (against) plus agonistes: the one who struggles against the protagonist.

steps.title: Compare the options
steps.body: An agnostic doubts that God can be known, a matter of belief, not of a story role. An arsonist sets fires. An anarchist rejects government. None of these is a character role. Antagonist is the opponent of the protagonist in the same story.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The antonym is antagonist, option (B).

shortcut.body: Recall the pair "protagonist versus antagonist", the stock opposition in story vocabulary. The three other options all start with the letter a and are decoys built to look like it. Under 20 seconds.

traps.text: Agnostic shares the prefix a- and the sound -gnostic/-agonist, so a candidate who matches letters instead of meaning picks it.
Arsonist begins with ars- and ends in -ist like protagonist. It is a pure sound-alike with no link to story roles.
Anarchist suggests "anti-establishment" and so feels opposed to a "leader", but a protagonist is a story role, not a ruler.

recognize.clues: The word protagonist has Greek parts (protos, first, and agonistes, contestant), and the question asks for its opposite inside the same domain of story roles.
recognize.contrast: A contextual-vocabulary question gets its meaning from a sentence around the blank. Here there is no sentence, so the word parts and the stock pairing decide.

check.body: Rebuild the word from its parts. Replace the prefix meaning first by the prefix meaning against, keep the contestant part, and you get the word for one who struggles against the leader. Exactly one option contains that contestant root.

hints.text: What role does a protagonist play in a story, and who stands on the other side of that role?
Many English words are built from Greek parts, and the parts often show the role the word names. Split protagonist into its two parts.
An antonym stays in the same domain and reverses the direction. Look for a storytelling word that takes the opposing side, not for a word that merely starts with the same letter.
Decide for each option whether it names a role in a story at all. Among the roles, pick the one that works against the leading character.
Say in one line what a protagonist wants in a story. Then ask which option could be the person who stands in the way of that.

variation.stem: The antonym of the word benefactor is ________.
variation.explanation: Benefactor joins bene (good) with factor (one who does), so it means one who does good. Swapping bene for male (bad) gives malefactor, one who does wrong. Benefactress is the same role for a woman, so it is no opposite, and the other two only share the letters fact.

questions.stem:
Despite his initial hesitation, Rehman’s _________ to contribute to the success of the project never wavered.

Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.

steps.title: How a fill-in-the-blank is decided
steps.body: A blank has to satisfy two tests: the word must fit the grammar of the slot, and its meaning must agree with the logic of the sentence. A connector such as "despite" reverses expectation: what follows it contrasts with what came before. Read the clues around the blank first, then test each option.

steps.title: Read the clues
steps.body: The sentence says Rehman first hesitated, "despite" which something about his wish to contribute "never wavered". To waver is to be unsteady. So the blank names a steady inner quality directed at contributing: a firm determination. The slot is a noun, because "Rehman’s ___" takes a noun and "to contribute" completes it.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Ambivalence means holding mixed or opposite feelings, which is a form of wavering and contradicts "never wavered". Satisfaction is a feeling of contentment and does not pair with "to contribute". Revolve is a verb meaning to turn around a centre, so it fails the grammar of the slot. Resolve, as a noun, means firm determination, and "resolve to contribute" is a standard phrase.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The correct word is resolve, option (C).

shortcut.body: Identify the part of speech needed (a noun) and the meaning needed (steadiness against hesitation). Resolve is the only noun that means firmness. Under 30 seconds.

traps.text: Ambivalence sounds like a fitting word for hesitation, so it is tempting after reading only the first half of the sentence. It is the very thing that "never wavered" denies.
Satisfaction is a plausible noun for a project’s success, but "satisfaction to contribute" is not idiomatic and it does not match "never wavered".
Revolve differs from resolve by one letter. Candidates who skim read it as resolve, but it is a verb and gives a meaningless sentence.

recognize.clues: 'Despite' sets hesitation against a quality that 'never wavered'. The blank follows a possessive and precedes 'to contribute', so it needs a noun for firm determination.
recognize.contrast: Do not choose by sound. Two options look alike but differ in part of speech and sense, and one option means mixed feelings, which is the very wavering the sentence denies.

check.body: Substitute each noun back and read the whole sentence. One option gives a sentence that contradicts itself, because it names wavering and then says nothing wavered. Another gives a phrase that no one says before 'to contribute'. Only one reads as a natural statement of steady commitment.

hints.text: What does 'never wavered' say about the quality the blank names, and how does 'despite his initial hesitation' set it against the first clause?
A blank must satisfy two tests together: it must fit the grammar of its slot and agree with the logic of the sentence.
A connector like despite signals contrast. The blank should be the opposite of the hesitation in the first clause, not a match for it.
Check the slot first: after a possessive and before 'to contribute', what part of speech is needed? Then keep only options of that kind whose meaning is firm and steady.
One option is a verb meaning to turn around a centre. A verb cannot follow Rehman's here, so it can be dropped.

variation.stem:
Despite the heavy rain, the volunteers' ________ to finish the clean-up never weakened.

Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
variation.explanation: Despite signals that the volunteers kept going, and never weakened needs a noun of steady purpose after the possessive. Determination fits. Doubt is the very wavering the sentence denies, destination only sounds close, and relief is a feeling that does not take 'to finish'.

questions.stem:
Ravi had ______ younger brother who taught at ______ university. He was widely regarded as ______ honorable man.

Select the option with the correct sequence of articles to fill in the blanks.

steps.title: What an article is and the rule for a versus an
steps.body: The articles are a, an and the. The indefinite article introduces one unspecified member of a class: a is used before a word that begins with a consonant sound, an before a word that begins with a vowel sound. The rule follows pronunciation, not spelling. Say the next word aloud and listen to its first sound. The definite article the points to one particular thing already known to both speaker and listener.

steps.title: Blank 1: younger
steps.body: Ravi had one younger brother, a new fact about him, so the indefinite article is right: "a younger brother" (with several brothers possible, the sentence does not say which). Younger begins with the sound /j/, a consonant sound, so the article is a.

steps.title: Blank 2: university
steps.body: Although university starts with the letter u, it is pronounced /ju:/, which begins with the consonant sound /j/. So the article is a: "a university".

steps.title: Blank 3: honorable
steps.body: The h of honorable is silent, so the word begins with the vowel sound /ɒ/. So the article is an: "an honorable man". The sequence is a; a; an, option (A).

shortcut.body: Check only the sounds of the three following words: younger (consonant), university (consonant /j/), honorable (silent h, vowel). That gives a, a, an. The second blank alone eliminates (B), (C) and (D) at once, since all three use an or the there. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: "the; an; a" fails on all three blanks: the is wrong for a newly mentioned brother, and an before university and a before honorable are both reversed by spelling-based reasoning.
Choosing an before university because it starts with the letter u, and a before honorable because it starts with the letter h. The rule is about sound, so both are reversed.
An before younger is wrong because younger starts with a consonant sound. Candidates who put an everywhere "to be safe" also pick this.

recognize.clues: Three blanks to fill with articles, options that differ only in sequence, and three following words (younger, university, honorable) whose first sound differs from what their spelling suggests.
recognize.contrast: The letter rule says a vowel letter takes an. It fails here: university starts with a vowel letter but a consonant sound, and honorable starts with a consonant letter but a vowel sound.

check.body: Read blank 2 aloud both ways: a university and an university. The second forces a vowel sound before the /j/ that university really starts with, so every option with an before university is out. That leaves one option, and reading its blanks aloud gives a younger, a university, an honorable.

hints.text: For each blank, what is the sound at the start of the very next word, not its first letter?
The article a goes before a consonant sound and an goes before a vowel sound. The rule follows pronunciation, so say the word aloud.
The points to something already known to both speaker and listener. A first mention of one unspecified person or thing takes a or an.
Take the blanks one at a time: younger, university, honorable. Write down whether the first sound of each is a consonant sound or a vowel sound, ignoring spelling.
Younger begins with the sound heard in 'yes', which is a consonant sound, so the first blank takes the article used before consonant sounds.

variation.stem:
Maya bought ______ umbrella, then met ______ European tourist who praised ______ hour-long performance.

Select the option with the correct sequence of articles to fill in the blanks.
variation.explanation: Umbrella begins with the vowel sound of uh, so an. European begins with the consonant sound of yoo, so a. Hour has a silent h and begins with a vowel sound, so an. Two options trust the first letter: an European and a hour come from reading letters, not sounds. The option with a before umbrella ignores that umbrella starts with a vowel sound.

questions.stem:
The CEO’s decision to downsize the workforce was considered myopic because it sacrificed long-term stability to accommodate short-term gains.

Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word “myopic” without changing the meaning of the sentence.

steps.title: How replacement questions work
steps.body: A replacement question asks for a synonym that keeps the sentence meaning intact. Find the word’s meaning from its roots or from the context, then confirm the replacement against the sentence’s own logic: the reason clause after "because" must still justify the word.

steps.title: Meaning of the word
steps.body: Myopia is the medical term for nearsightedness, the inability to see distant things clearly. Used figuratively, myopic describes a person who fails to look ahead and sees only what is near in time. The sentence gives the reason itself: the decision traded long-term stability for short-term gains, which is exactly failing to look far ahead.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Visionary means having a clear long-range view, the opposite. Progressive means favouring reform and forward movement, and innovative means introducing new methods; neither says anything about ignoring the future, and a decision that sacrifices long-term stability would not be praised with them. Shortsighted means lacking foresight, the exact figurative sense of myopic.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The replacement is shortsighted, option (B).

shortcut.body: The sentence defines the word for you: "sacrificed long-term stability for short-term gains" is the definition of shortsighted. Also recall that myopia means nearsightedness. Under 20 seconds.

traps.text: Visionary is the exact antonym. It is chosen by candidates who do not know the word and pick the "business-sounding" option.
Progressive sounds like a corporate term for a restructuring decision, but it carries a positive tone that clashes with the criticism in the sentence.
Innovative is a favourable word for novel decisions. The sentence calls the decision a mistake, so a praising word cannot replace myopic.

recognize.clues: The word sits in quotation marks with a request to replace it, and the 'because' clause (long-term stability traded for short-term gains) defines it through context.
recognize.contrast: A word-roots question relies on the parts of the word alone. Here the sentence's own reason clause confirms the meaning, so check the replacement against the sentence as well as the root.

check.body: Substitute each option into the sentence and ask whether the 'because' clause still justifies it. Trading long-term stability for short-term gains justifies a word of criticism about foresight. It cannot justify a word that praises the decision, so those contradict the clause.

hints.text: What does the clause after 'because' say the CEO did, and what kind of thinking does that describe?
The word starts as a medical term about eyesight. Used figuratively, it carries the same picture over to judgement.
A replacement must keep the full meaning of the sentence, including its criticism. A word of praise cannot stand in for a word used to criticise a decision.
Sort the options by whether they would praise or criticise the decision. Keep the ones that match the tone of the sentence and test them against the reason clause.
In medicine, this condition means seeing what is near clearly and what is far poorly. Carry that picture over to a decision about time.

variation.stem:
The board's decision to keep a reserve fund was considered prudent because it prepared the firm for lean years.

Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word “prudent” without changing the meaning of the sentence.
variation.explanation: The reason clause says the decision prepared the firm for hard times, which is good judgement about the future. Sensible keeps that meaning. Reckless is the opposite, generous is about giving, and secretive is about hiding information.

questions.stem:
“I put the brown paper in my pocket along with the chalks, and possibly other things. I suppose every one must have reflected how primeval and how poetical are the things that one carries in one’s pocket: the pocket-knife, for instance the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword. Once I planned to write a book of poems entirely about the things in my pocket. But I found it would be too long: and the age of the great epics is past.”

(From G.K. Chesterton’s “A Piece of Chalk”)

Based only on the information provided in the above passage, which one of the following statements is true?
options: The author of the passage carries a mirror in his pocket to reflect upon things.
The author of the passage had decided to write a poem on epics.
The pocket-knife is described as the infant of the sword.
Epics are described as too inconvenient to write.

steps.title: The rule for "based only on the passage" questions
steps.body: A statement is true only if the passage states it, or it follows with no outside knowledge. Treat each option as a claim and look for the exact words in the passage that support or contradict it. A claim that is merely plausible, or that reuses a word from the passage in a new sense, is false for this purpose. Strong words and changed details are the usual signs of a planted false option.

steps.title: Collect what the passage actually says
steps.body: The author carries brown paper, chalks and possibly other things. People have "reflected" on how primeval and poetical pocket things are. The pocket-knife is called "the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword". The author once planned a book of poems about pocket things, found it would be too long, and says the age of great epics is past.

steps.title: Check each option against those facts
steps.body: (A) "Reflected" here means thought about, not mirror-reflected; no mirror is mentioned. (B) The planned book was of poems about pocket things; epics are mentioned only as a past age. (C) The text calls the pocket-knife "the infant of the sword", word for word. (D) The book would be "too long", not inconvenient, and the line about epics is a separate remark that the epic age has passed.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (C) is stated by the passage, so the answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Scan the passage for a phrase that an option copies exactly. "Infant of the sword" appears in the text and in option (C) only. For the others, find the changed word: mirror, epics, inconvenient. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: The pun on "reflected" (thought versus mirror) is the planted lure. The passage never mentions a mirror.
It mixes up two facts: the poems were to be about pocket things, and epics are only mentioned as belonging to the past.
The passage says the book would be too long, not that epics are inconvenient. It also never describes epics as a task the author attempted.

recognize.clues: 'Based only on the information provided' with four claims built from passage words. One copies a phrase of the text, and the others change a detail or twist a word.
recognize.contrast: A main-idea question asks what the whole passage is about. Here the task is to verify each claim against the text, so one changed word is enough to make an option false.

check.body: Take a second route through the wrong options. For each one, find the passage sentence it distorts and name the changed detail: a mirror for a thought, a poem on epics for poems about pocket things, inconvenient for too long. The true option is the only one where no detail has been changed.

hints.text: For each option, can you point to the exact words in the passage that say it?
In a 'based only on the passage' question, a statement is true only if the passage states it or it follows directly with no outside knowledge.
Watch for options that reuse a passage word in a different sense or change one detail. A reused word is not evidence.
Take each option, underline its key noun (mirror, epics, pocket-knife, inconvenient), and search the passage for that noun with the same claim attached.
Try the first option: search the passage for any mention of a mirror. If none is there, the option rests on a pun and cannot be supported.

variation.stem:
The harbour clock stopped at noon on the day the ferry was cancelled. Old Marta, who kept the key, said she had never once been late to wind it, and that she would rather let the town lose an hour than hand the key to a stranger. By evening nobody trusted any clock but the church bell.

Based only on the information provided in the above passage, which one of the following statements is true?
options: Marta handed the key to a stranger.
The ferry was cancelled on the day the clock stopped.
Marta admitted she was sometimes late to wind the clock.
The church bell stopped at noon.
variation.explanation: The first sentence states the clock stopped on the day the ferry was cancelled. The first option reverses Marta's refusal, the third contradicts her claim of never being late, and the fourth moves the stopping from the clock to the bell, which the passage says people trusted.

questions.stem:
If ‘→’ denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words

[walk → jog → sprint] is analogous to [bothered → ________ → daunted].

Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?

steps.title: What the question is
steps.body: It is an analogy on a scale: three words that are the same kind of thing and rise in intensity. The first scale (walk, jog, sprint) is three speeds of the same movement. The blank must be a word that sits between bothered and daunted on a scale of how much something unsettles a person.

steps.title: Build the second scale
steps.body: To be bothered is to be mildly annoyed or disturbed. To be daunted is to be made fearful or discouraged by something big. A word in the middle should mean unsettled or disconcerted, stronger than bothered but weaker than daunted.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Fazed means disturbed or thrown off balance, usually in the negative "not fazed by". It fits the middle of the scale. Phased means done in stages. Phrased means expressed in words. Fused means joined together by melting. The last three are real words that sound like fazed but belong to other meanings.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The blank is fazed, option (C).

shortcut.body: Three of the options are sound-alikes (phased, phrased, fused); only one of the four describes an emotional state at all. Pick the state word that is neither mild nor extreme. Under 40 seconds.

traps.text: Phased is pronounced the same as fazed. A candidate who matches sound, or who has only heard the word, picks it. It means carried out in stages.
Phrased looks like fazed in the first letters and in length, but it is about wording.
Fused is a fourth sound-alike that has no link to an emotion.

recognize.clues: The arrow notation says 'increasing order of intensity', the walk, jog, sprint triple shows the pattern, and the blank sits in the middle of a scale of how much something unsettles a person.
recognize.contrast: A plain synonym question has no ordering. Here the blank must also rank between its neighbours, so a word of similar meaning that is too weak or too strong would still be wrong.

check.body: Put the answer in a sentence: the noise bothered him, the size of the task fazed him, and finally it daunted him. The rise is smooth and fazed means thrown off balance. Now try a sound-alike in the middle: the size of the task phased him does not make sense, because phased means done in stages.

hints.text: What do walk, jog and sprint have in common, and how must the second scale mirror it?
An intensity analogy places three words of one kind in rising order. The middle word must be stronger than the first and weaker than the last.
Words that sound alike are still different words. Decide by meaning, and ask whether the candidate describes a feeling or state of a person.
Describe the scale in plain words: bothered is mildly disturbed and daunted is strongly discouraged. Then ask which option names a state of being unsettled that sits between them.
Test the first option in 'The bad news phased her.' Does the sentence say how she felt?

variation.stem:
If ‘→’ denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [sip → gulp → guzzle] is analogous to [tired → ________ → exhausted].

Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
variation.explanation: Sip, gulp and guzzle rise in how much is drunk at once. Tired, weary, exhausted rise in how drained a person is, and weary sits between them. Wary means cautious, merry means cheerful, and worry is a verb or noun for anxiety. Only weary describes tiredness.

questions.stem:
Sequence the following sentences in a coherent passage.

P: This fortuitous geological event generated a colossal amount of energy and heat that resulted in the rocks rising to an average height of 4 km across the contact zone.

Q: Thus, the geophysicists tend to think of the Himalayas as an active geological event rather than as a static geological feature.

R: The natural process of the cooling of this massive edifice absorbed large quantities of atmospheric carbon dioxide, altering the earth’s atmosphere and making it better suited for life.

S: Many millennia ago, a breakaway chunk of bedrock from the Antarctic Plate collided with the massive Eurasian Plate.

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain S to P to R to Q. Each arrow is labelled with the phrase in the later sentence that points back to the earlier one.

steps.title: The method for sequencing
steps.body: A coherent paragraph has an opening sentence that stands alone, and every later sentence leans on an earlier one through a pointer: "this", "these", "thus", "however", a pronoun, or a definite noun phrase. Identify the sentence that needs nothing before it, then chain the rest by following who points to whom. Words like "thus" and "therefore" mark conclusions and go last.

steps.title: Find the opener
steps.body: S introduces the collision with an indefinite phrase "Many millennia ago, a breakaway chunk of bedrock", which is a first mention and needs no antecedent. P begins "This fortuitous geological event", which points back to something. R says "this massive edifice", and Q begins "Thus". So S opens the passage.

steps.title: Chain the rest
steps.body: P follows S: "this event" is the collision, and P describes its energy and the rising rocks. R follows P: "this massive edifice" is the mass of risen rock created in P, and R describes its cooling. Q comes last: "Thus" draws a conclusion from all that precedes, about how geophysicists view the Himalayas.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The order S, P, R, Q is option (C). The drawing shows each pointer phrase.

shortcut.body: Find the opener (the sentence with no pointer) and the closer (the "Thus"). That is S first and Q last, which leaves only SPRQ and SRPQ. Then ask whether the edifice can be cooling before it has risen: P before R. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: QPSR starts with "Thus", a conclusion with nothing before it to conclude from.
QSPR also opens with Q for the same reason.
SRPQ gets the opener right and the closer right but places R, which talks about "this massive edifice", before P has built it.

recognize.clues: Four lettered sentences to order. S has an indefinite first mention, P and R open with 'This fortuitous geological event' and 'this massive edifice', and Q opens with 'Thus'.
recognize.contrast: A transition-signals question asks for a connector to fill a gap. Here the connectors and pointers fix the order of whole sentences instead.

check.body: Read the order aloud and test each seam: a collision, then the energy that lifts the rocks, then the cooling of the risen mass, then the conclusion. Swap the middle two and the mass would cool before the rocks ever rose to form it, which is impossible.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 GA question 6
GATE 2024 CS2 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: Which sentence could open the paragraph without any earlier sentence to explain it?
In a sequencing question, pointer words such as this, thus and these refer back to something earlier, so a sentence that begins with one cannot come first.
A conclusion marker such as 'thus' belongs near the end, after the facts that lead to it. A first mention uses an indefinite phrase, and a later mention uses 'this' or 'the'.
Mark each sentence as an opener (no pointer) or a follower (has a pointer). For each pointer, name the earlier sentence it must refer to.
R speaks of 'this massive edifice'. Of the other three sentences, which one builds something massive for R to refer to?

variation.stem:
Sequence the following sentences in a coherent passage.

P: Thus the squirrel, while only storing food, ends up planting the forest.

Q: In autumn, a grey squirrel buries hundreds of acorns across a wide territory.

R: But some are never found, and these forgotten acorns sprout in spring into young oak trees.

S: Over the winter it digs up most of them to eat.
variation.explanation: Q opens because it introduces the squirrel and the acorns with no pointer. S follows, since 'it' and 'them' need Q, and R follows S because 'But some are never found' contrasts with most being dug up. P closes with 'Thus'. Putting R before S would have acorns sprouting in spring before the winter digging, so QRSP fails on time order.

questions.stem:
If ‘→’ denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words

[dry → arid → parched] is analogous to [diet → fast → ________ ].

Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?

steps.title: What the arrow means
steps.body: The arrow orders three words by intensity, so each word is a stronger version of the same underlying quantity. In the first scale the quantity is lack of water: dry, then arid, then parched. To fill the second scale, name its quantity and find the word at the extreme end.

steps.title: Find the quantity in the second scale
steps.body: To diet is to eat less on purpose. To fast is to go without food for a period, a stronger restriction. The quantity is how little food a person takes in, and the next step up is to take in almost none or none at all.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Starve means to suffer or die from lack of food, the extreme of the scale. Reject and deny are verbs of refusal in general, with no link to the amount of food. Feast means to eat a great deal, the opposite direction.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The blank is starve, option (A).

shortcut.body: Name the scale in two words ("less food") and move one step further. Feast runs the wrong way and reject and deny do not mention food. Under 30 seconds.

traps.text: Reject has the feel of "refuse food" but it is not tied to food or to degree, so it fits no point on the scale.
Feast is a food word, and a hurried reader picks it as the "food ending". It reverses the direction of the scale.
Deny can follow "diet" in the sense of denying oneself, but it does not mark a stronger stage than fasting.

recognize.clues: The arrow is defined as increasing intensity and the first list is a three-step scale, so the task is to copy that scale pattern onto diet and fast.
recognize.contrast: A plain synonym or antonym analogy has one pair and one relation; here the relation is a ranked scale, so the blank must go further than the last word, not merely mean the same.

check.body: Reverse test: read the second list backwards, starve then fast then diet. Each step eats a little more, which matches parched then arid then dry getting less severe, so the order holds.

The blank must sit one step beyond the last word on the same scale, in the same direction, and must be a word that belongs to that scale at all.
Diet means eating less on purpose, and fast means eating even less for a spell. Ask what word names the limit of eating less.
Drop the options that reverse the direction of the scale and the ones that say nothing about food.

variation.stem: If the arrow denotes increasing order of intensity, then [warm → hot → scorching] is analogous to [cool → cold → ________]. Which option fits the blank?
variation.explanation: The scale is how low the temperature is, rising in intensity. Freezing names the extreme end beyond cold. Warm runs the opposite way, mild is weaker than cold, and sunny describes light, not temperature.

questions.stem:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)−(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.

Steve was advised to keep his head (i) ____ before heading (ii) ____ to bat; for, while he had a head (iii) ____ batting, he could only do so with a cool head (iv) ____ his shoulders.

steps.title: How idiom blanks work
steps.body: Many English phrases are fixed: swapping the small word (a preposition or particle) changes the meaning or produces nonsense. Solve a multi-blank question by recalling the fixed phrase behind each blank and then keep the option that satisfies all four, not just one.

steps.title: Recall the four fixed phrases
steps.body: (i) "keep your head down" means stay low and focused, out of trouble. (ii) "head out" means to set off, so "before heading out to bat" means before going out to the crease. (iii) "have a head for" something means to have an aptitude for it, so "a head for batting" is a talent for batting. (iv) "a cool head on one’s shoulders" means a calm, sensible mind.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The sequence is down, out, for, on. Option (A) fails at (ii) and (iii), (B) fails at (i) and (ii), and (D) fails at (i) and (iv). Only (C) gives all four fixed phrases.

shortcut.body: Start with the surest idiom: (iv) "a cool head on his shoulders" needs on, which leaves (B) and (C). Then (i) "keep his head down" rules out (B), leaving (C). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: (A) repeats down in "heading down to bat", and "a head on batting" and "a cool head for his shoulders" are not idioms.
"Keep his head on" is not the idiom, and "heading down to bat" lacks the sense of going out to the crease; (ii) needs out.
"Head on" in (i) means face-to-face, and "a cool head for his shoulders" in (iv) is the reverse of the idiom.

recognize.clues: Four blanks hide only small words (down, out, for, on) inside head phrases, so each blank is a fixed idiom about the word head.
recognize.contrast: Plain grammar questions on prepositions follow a general rule; here the pairing is memorised phrase by phrase, so no rule decides it.

check.body: Read the finished sentence aloud: keep his head down before heading out to bat, a head for batting, a cool head on his shoulders. Each phrase is a standard idiom, and swapping any one word breaks it.

questions.stem: We reached the station late, and _______ missed the train.

steps.title: What the blank must be
steps.body: A word that modifies a verb ("missed") is an adverb. An adverb here also has to match the logic of the sentence. First settle the part of speech, then settle the meaning, and keep the option that passes both tests.

steps.title: Part of speech
steps.body: Near is an adjective, a preposition or a place-adverb ("the near shore", "near the station", "stood near"), but it cannot express degree ("almost") before a past-tense verb. Nearly, utterly and mostly are -ly adverbs of degree, so they stay.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: "Reached the station late, and ___ missed the train" sets up a near thing: lateness put the train at risk, and the speaker only came close to missing it. Nearly means almost, so "nearly missed" says the miss was avoided by a small margin. Utterly means completely and mostly means for the most part; neither describes a single event that did or did not happen, and "utterly" would contradict the natural reading.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The word is nearly, option (B).

shortcut.body: Strike near (it cannot mean "almost" before a verb), then choose between the adverbs by meaning: a single past event is "nearly" done or not, never "mostly" done. Under 20 seconds.

traps.text: Near feels close to nearly and is often confused with it, but it is not an adverb of degree.
Utterly means completely, an intensifier that suggests a total miss and mismatches the narrow-margin idea.
Mostly means for the most part, used with groups or amounts, not with one event.

recognize.clues: A single blank before the verb missed, with four look-alike words from one family of sense, so the blank is settled by part of speech and then meaning.
recognize.contrast: Near and nearly look alike but near is mainly an adjective or preposition; only nearly gives the idea of almost before a verb.

check.body: Substitute each candidate and read it aloud. We nearly missed the train is natural English. We near missed the train and we mostly missed the train are not. Utterly is an adverb, but it changes a close call into a certain miss, and the lateness only sets up a close call, so nearly is the one option that is both an adverb before the verb and means almost.

hints.text: What kind of word is needed before the verb missed, and what does the sentence say actually happened to the train?

Being late puts the train at risk. Ask which options say the miss nearly happened, and which say how completely or how often.

variation.explanation: The blank needs a degree adverb meaning almost before the verb dropped. Nearly gives that sense. Nearby is a place word, hardly means scarcely and reverses the meaning, and merely means only.

questions.stem:
Kind : _______ : : Often : Frequently

(By word meaning)
questions.keyNote: The official final key awards marks to all. GATE Overflow records that the first key gave (B) Type, then the institute changed it to marks to all. The discussion shows why the stem is flawed: Kind has several senses, as a noun it means Type, and as an adjective or adverb Kindly can also be argued as its synonym. Because the stem allows two defensible completions, no single option is correct. Our answer (B) is the intended one.

steps.title: What the analogy means
steps.body: The notation A : B :: C : D says the relation between A and B is the same as between C and D. The note "By word meaning" says the relation is about meaning. So first name the relation in the complete pair, then find the option that stands in the same relation to Kind.

steps.title: Name the relation
steps.body: Often and Frequently both mean "many times". They are synonyms. So the blank must be a synonym of Kind.

steps.title: Find the synonym
steps.body: Kind has two common senses. As an adjective it means gentle and caring, and the opposites of that are Mean and Cruel. As a noun it means a class or sort of thing, and its synonym is Type ("what kind of book" and "what type of book" mean the same). Mean and Cruel are antonyms of the first sense, so they are out. Kindly shares the root and the gentle sense, but it is a derived form, not a plain synonym.

steps.title: Answer and the key
steps.body: The intended answer is Type, option (B). The official key later awarded marks to all, because Kindly could also be defended.

shortcut.body: Turn the pair into a rule ("synonym"), cross out antonyms (Mean, Cruel), then pick the plain synonym: Type. The official outcome was marks to all, so do not lose time on this type of ambiguity in the hall. Under 40 seconds.

traps.text: Mean is the antonym of kind in the sense of gentle, so it breaks the synonym rule.
Cruel is another antonym of kind, so it breaks the relation.
Kindly looks like the answer because it shares the root, and the key gave marks to all because it is arguable. It is a derived adverb, not the plain synonym that the relation asks for.

recognize.clues: The pair Often : Frequently fixes a synonym relation, and the note by word meaning limits the match to meaning, not form.
recognize.contrast: An antonym analogy has the same layout but opposite words; test the complete pair first to tell which relation is asked. Note the official outcome here was marks to all, so the stem is ambiguous.

check.body: Swap test: put the candidate into the sentence what ___ of book is this, and into the pair Often : Frequently. If the word can be exchanged with Kind in that way the relation holds. Mean and Cruel fail it, as they reverse the sense of gentle.

hints.text: What relation links the two complete words, Often and Frequently, and how would you describe it in one word?

Rule out any option that stands to the first word in a different relation, for example an opposite, before comparing the remaining options by sense.

questions.stem:
Which one of the following sentence sequences creates a coherent narrative?

(i) Once on the terrace, on her way to her small room in the corner, she notices the man right away.
(ii) She begins to pant by the time she has climbed all the stairs.
(iii) Mina has bought vegetables and rice at the market, so her bags are heavy.
(iv) He was leaning against the parapet, watching the traffic below.

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain iii to ii to i to iv. Labels on the arrows name the clue: heavy bags explain the panting, the climb ends on the terrace, noticing the man introduces he.

steps.title: The method
steps.body: A narrative has one order in which time and reference both work. First find the sentence that introduces the characters by name, since a pronoun ("she", "he") cannot come before the person it stands for. Then order the events by time and by cause: a cause comes before its effect, and a place reached comes after the journey to it.

steps.title: The opener
steps.body: Sentence (iii) names Mina and gives the situation, heavy bags, so it opens. Sentences (ii) and (i) use "she" and (iv) uses "he", all pronouns that need earlier mentions.

steps.title: Chain the events
steps.body: The heavy bags explain why Mina pants after climbing the stairs, so (ii) follows (iii). Climbing all the stairs ends on the terrace, which is where (i) starts ("once on the terrace"). In (i) she notices "the man", and (iv) then describes him ("He was leaning..."), so (iv) closes the sequence.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The order is (iii), (ii), (i), (iv), option (D). Option (A) has her notice the man before she has climbed, and ends with the shopping. Option (B) opens with "She" before Mina is named. Option (C) opens with "He", who has not been introduced.

shortcut.body: The only sentence with a name and no pronoun is (iii). Only (D) starts with it. Check the rest in ten seconds. About 1 minute.

traps.text: It starts with the arrival on the terrace, then climbs the stairs afterwards, and ends with shopping, which breaks time order.
It opens with "She" with nobody named, and it puts (iii) after the panting, so the cause comes after the effect.
It opens with "He", whom the reader has not met, and shows the climb after the sight on the terrace.

recognize.clues: Four loose sentences with she, he and a named person (Mina) in only one of them, plus cause and place links such as heavy bags and once on the terrace.
recognize.contrast: Paragraph sequencing by theme alone needs topic sentences; this one is solved by who is introduced first and by cause and place.

check.body: Read the chosen order as a story: Mina has heavy bags, pants after the stairs, reaches the terrace, notices the man, who is leaning on the parapet. Every pronoun has an earlier referent and no event comes before its cause.

questions.stem: The _________ is too high for it to be considered _________.

steps.title: Homophones
steps.body: Homophones are words that sound the same and are spelled differently, with different meanings. Here the pair is fare and fair. Fare is a noun: the money charged for a journey. Fair is an adjective meaning reasonable or just. Decide each blank by its part of speech first and by meaning second.

steps.title: Blank 1
steps.body: "The ___ is too high" needs a noun that can be high. A price is high, so the noun is fare: the charge for the ride.

steps.title: Blank 2
steps.body: "Too high for it to be considered ___" needs an adjective that describes a charge: reasonable and just, which is fair.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The sentence is "The fare is too high for it to be considered fair", option (D). Option (B) contains faer, which is not a word.

shortcut.body: Blank 1 is a noun (money), so it must be fare; that leaves (C) and (D). Blank 2 is an adjective, so fair. Under 20 seconds.

traps.text: It reverses both words, which happens when a candidate remembers the two spellings but not which is the noun.
Faer is not a word, so any option containing it fails, even though its second blank (fair) is right.
Fare in both blanks fixes blank 1 but "considered fare" is not a sensible description of a charge.

recognize.clues: Two blanks filled by the same two sounds in different spellings, so the sentence meaning and the part of speech decide each blank.
recognize.contrast: Spelling confusion between homophones differs from near-synonym choice, since here only one spelling fits a given part of speech.

check.body: Read the result and substitute meanings: the money charged is too high for it to be considered reasonable. The sentence stays logical, whereas the swapped version, the reasonable is too high, does not.

questions.stem:
Some people believe that “what gets measured, improves”. Some others believe that “what gets measured, gets gamed”. One possible reason for the difference in the beliefs is the work culture in organizations. In organizations with good work culture, metrics help improve outcomes. However, the same metrics are counterproductive in organizations with poor work culture.

Which one of the following is the CORRECT logical inference based on the information in the above passage?
options: Metrics are useful in organizations with poor work culture
Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture
Metrics are always counterproductive in organizations with good work culture
Metrics are never useful in organizations with good work culture

steps.title: How an inference question is decided
steps.body: The correct inference is one that must be true given the passage alone. Write the passage as plain conditions, then test every option against them. An option that contradicts a condition is out, and an option that adds a strong word such as "always" or "never" that the passage does not support is also out.

steps.title: Write the conditions
steps.body: If the work culture is good, metrics help improve outcomes. If it is poor, the same metrics are counterproductive. Those are the only two facts.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) says metrics are useful under poor culture, which is the opposite of the second condition. (B) says metrics are useful under good culture; "help improve outcomes" is the same claim. (C) says metrics are always counterproductive under good culture, which contradicts the first condition. (D) says never useful under good culture, which also contradicts it.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (B) is supported, so the answer is (B).

shortcut.body: Reduce the passage to two lines (good culture: helps, poor culture: hurts) and match option to line. Three options swap or negate the lines. About 1 minute.

traps.text: It swaps the cultures: the passage says metrics backfire under poor culture.
It claims metrics always backfire under good culture, the reverse of what the passage says.
"Never useful" under good culture contradicts "help improve outcomes". Absolute words in an option need a direct line of support.

recognize.clues: The question stem says correct logical inference based on the passage, and the options differ by swapped conditions and strong words like always and never.
recognize.contrast: A main-idea question asks for the overall point; an inference question accepts only what the text directly supports, so a plausible extra claim is wrong.

check.body: Negation test: if the chosen option were false, the passage would say that metrics fail to help in a good culture, which it explicitly denies. The other three each conflict with a stated condition.

An inference question asks what must be true from the passage alone, not what is likely or what you know yourself.

Write two lines: what happens to metrics with good work culture, and what happens with poor work culture. Match each option to a line.

questions.stem: Gauri said that she can play the keyboard __________ her sister.

steps.title: The frame for an equal comparison
steps.body: A comparison of equality says that two people have the same degree of a quality. English builds it with a fixed frame: as + a word in its plain form + as. The plain form is the word with no -er, no -est and no more or most, for example well, good, tall, fast. The frame already carries the comparison, so the word inside must not carry a second one. Better and worse are comparative forms, and nicest is a superlative form, so none of them can sit between the two as.

steps.title: Read what the sentence claims
steps.body: Gauri says her keyboard playing matches her sister's. That is a claim of equality, so the blank must hold the whole frame as + plain word + as. The word in the middle describes how she plays, which makes it an adverb, and the plain adverb for good playing is well.

steps.title: Test each option against the frame
steps.body: (A) as well as: plain adverb inside the frame, correct. (B) as better as: better is comparative, so the comparison is marked twice; the comparative frame is better than. (C) as nicest as: nicest is a superlative, which needs the nicest of a group, and nice does not describe how someone plays. (D) as worse as: worse is comparative, so it breaks the frame in the same way as (B).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (A) completes the equal-comparison frame, so the answer is (A).

shortcut.body: Look at the word between the two as. If it ends in -er or -est, or is better, worse or best, strike it. Only well is left. Ten seconds. Safe whenever the blank sits between two as.

traps.text: Better sounds like the right word for a skilled player, but it already means "more good than". Put inside as ... as it marks the comparison twice. Its own frame is better than.
Nicest feels positive, so it attracts a reader who picks the most flattering word. It is a superlative, which compares one item with a whole group, and it does not describe playing.
Worse is a comparative, so it breaks the frame exactly as better does, and it also turns the claim into a negative one that the sentence gives no reason for.

recognize.clues: The blank sits between a verb phrase and her sister, in a claim of equal skill, so the as ... as frame is needed.
recognize.contrast: A comparative uses than after an -er word (better than); the equal frame uses two as with a plain word, so better never sits inside it.

check.body: Substitute plain words into the frame: as tall as, as fast as, as well as all work. Put in better or nicest and the frame fails, so the form of the middle word is the only test needed.

questions.stem:
Listening to music during exercise improves exercise performance and reduces discomfort. Scientists researched whether listening to music while studying can help students learn better and the results were inconclusive. Students who needed external stimulation for studying fared worse while students who did not need any external stimulation benefited from music.

Which one of the following statements is the CORRECT inference of the above passage?
options: Listening to music has no effect on learning and a positive effect on physical exercise.
Listening to music has a clear positive effect both on physical exercise and on learning.
Listening to music has a clear positive effect on physical exercise. Music has a positive effect on learning only in some students.
Listening to music has a clear positive effect on learning in all students. Music has a positive effect only in some students who exercise.

steps.title: What counts as a correct inference
steps.body: An inference is a statement that must be true if the passage is true. An option made of two sentences needs both of them supported, so check each sentence on its own. Strong words such as clear, no, all and only make a claim hard to support: the passage has to say that much, not merely hint at it.

steps.title: Pull out the facts, one topic at a time
steps.body: Exercise: music improves performance and reduces discomfort. The passage states this flatly, so a clear positive effect is supported. Learning: the overall result of the research was inconclusive, and it splits by student. Students who needed external stimulation fared worse; students who needed none benefited. So for learning the effect is positive for some students and negative for others.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) no effect on learning: the split shows real effects in both directions, and the passage never says there is none. (B) clear positive effect on learning: the passage calls the result inconclusive. (C) clear positive effect on exercise is stated, and a positive effect on learning for only some students matches the split. (D) clear positive effect on learning in all students: a student group fared worse, and the second sentence swaps the topics, since the exercise effect is not limited to some people.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Both sentences of (C) are supported and every other option fails at least one, so the answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Split every option into its exercise part and its learning part. All three of (A), (B), (C) accept the exercise claim, so the learning part decides. Inconclusive plus a split by student rules out clear, all and no effect, which leaves (C). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: It treats an inconclusive overall result as no effect. Inconclusive means the research did not settle one direction; here it did show effects, positive for some students and negative for others.
It carries the clear positive claim from exercise over to learning. The passage says the learning result was inconclusive, so a clear positive effect is not supported.
It gives the learning effect to all students, which the group that fared worse contradicts, and then moves the some-students limit onto exercise, where the passage sets no limit.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the CORRECT inference, each option has two sentences, and the options lean on strong words (clear, no, all, only). The passage calls the learning result inconclusive and splits it by kind of student.
recognize.contrast: A main-idea question wants the gist of the whole passage. Here each claim must be forced by a specific sentence, so you test the parts one by one.

check.body: Second route, by contradiction: find the passage phrase that breaks each rejected option. The students who benefited break the claim of no effect, the word inconclusive breaks a clear effect on learning, and the students who fared worse break an effect on all students. The kept option breaks no phrase.

hints.text: Split each option into its parts. What does the passage say separately about exercise and about studying?
An inference is something that has to be true given the passage, not something that merely sounds likely.
Words such as clear, no, all and only demand strong support. A mixed or inconclusive result cannot back a claim of that strength.
Write the passage's verdict on exercise and its verdict on learning side by side, then test every sentence of every option against them.
On learning, the passage reports a difference between kinds of student, so look for an option that does not treat all students alike.

variation.stem:
Caffeine before a race raises sprint speed and shortens reaction time. Researchers also tested whether caffeine helps people memorise word lists, and the results were mixed. Those who rarely drink coffee recalled more words, while heavy coffee drinkers recalled fewer.

Which one of the following statements is the CORRECT inference of the above passage?
options: Caffeine has a clear positive effect on memorising for everyone and no effect on sprinting.
Caffeine has no effect on memorising and a positive effect on sprinting.
Caffeine has a clear positive effect on both sprinting and memorising.
Caffeine has a clear positive effect on sprinting. Its effect on memorising is positive only for some people.
variation.explanation: Split each option by topic. Sprinting is stated flatly as improved, so a clear positive effect holds. Memorising is mixed and divides by coffee habit, which rules out no effect and an effect on everyone, and leaves the option that limits the benefit to some people.

questions.stem:
Consider the following sentences:

(i) Everybody in the class is prepared for the exam.
(ii) Babu invited Danish to his home because he enjoys playing chess.

Which of the following is the CORRECT observation about the above two sentences?
options: (i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is ambiguous
(i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is ambiguous

steps.title: Two rules, one for each sentence
steps.body: Agreement rule: indefinite pronouns such as everybody, everyone, somebody and each name a group but take a singular verb, so they pair with is, not are. Reference rule: a pronoun stands for an earlier noun, its antecedent. If two or more earlier nouns could be the antecedent, the sentence is ambiguous because the reader cannot tell which one is meant.

steps.title: Sentence (i)
steps.body: The subject is everybody, which is singular, and the verb is is. Prepared for the exam is a normal adjective phrase. The sentence is grammatically correct.

steps.title: Sentence (ii)
steps.body: The pronoun he follows the nouns Babu and Danish. Both are male and singular, so either can be the antecedent. Reading one: Babu invited Danish because Babu enjoys playing chess. Reading two: Babu invited Danish because Danish enjoys playing chess. Both readings make sense, so the sentence is ambiguous. Repeating the name, as in because Danish enjoys playing chess, removes the doubt.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Sentence (i) is correct and sentence (ii) is ambiguous, which is option (C).

shortcut.body: Check the two sentences separately. In (i) the verb matches a singular everybody. In (ii) scan for a pronoun with two same-gender candidates before it, and he has two. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: It assumes he must refer to the subject Babu because the subject usually comes first. A pronoun may refer to the object too, and here the reason clause reads naturally for Danish.
It makes two mistakes: it reads everybody as plural because it means many people, and it misses the second antecedent in (ii).
It judges (i) wrong because everybody feels plural, since it points to many students. Grammar counts it as singular, so is is correct.

recognize.clues: Sentence (i) has the indefinite pronoun everybody with a verb to check. Sentence (ii) has the pronoun he after two male names. Each option pairs a grammar verdict with a clarity verdict.
recognize.contrast: Plain subject-verb agreement settles sentence (i) only. Sentence (ii) is a reference problem: the pronoun has the right number but two possible antecedents, which is different from a pronoun of the wrong number.

check.body: Repair test: put Babu in place of he, then Danish. Both sentences read sensibly but mean different things, so the original does not fix one meaning. For (i), replace everybody with each student: each student is prepared is plainly singular, matching the verb in the sentence.

A pronoun stands in for an earlier noun, its antecedent. Indefinite pronouns such as everybody are treated as one unit by the verb.
Two checks decide it: the verb must agree in number with its subject, and a pronoun needs one clear antecedent. Two equally possible antecedents leave the sentence unclear.
For the first sentence, decide whether the subject is singular or plural and compare that with the verb. For the second, list every earlier noun that matches the pronoun in gender and number.
In the second sentence, list the earlier nouns the pronoun could refer to, then ask whether the reason clause reads sensibly about each one.

Consider the following sentences:

(i) Each of the players have signed the form.
(ii) Meera told Nisha that she had won the prize.

Which of the following is the CORRECT observation about the above two sentences?
options: (i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is ambiguous
(i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is ambiguous
variation.explanation: Each takes a singular verb, so have should be has and (i) is incorrect; the plural noun players next to the verb is the lure. In (ii) she can mean Meera or Nisha, both female and singular, so the reference is ambiguous.

questions.stem:
Some people suggest anti-obesity measures (AOM) such as displaying calorie information in restaurant menus. Such measures sidestep addressing the core problems that cause obesity: poverty and income inequality.

Which one of the following statements summarizes the passage?
options: The proposed AOM addresses the core problems that cause obesity.
If obesity reduces, poverty will naturally reduce, since obesity causes poverty.
AOM are addressing the core problems and are likely to succeed.
AOM are addressing the problem superficially.

steps.title: What a summary must do
steps.body: A summary restates the main claim of the passage in fewer words. It keeps the author's judgement and its direction, and it adds nothing and reverses nothing. A passage that first reports a proposal and then objects to it is summarised by the objection, because the objection is the author's point.

steps.title: Find the main claim
steps.body: The passage reports a proposal (anti-obesity measures such as calorie labels) and then says these measures sidestep the core problems, which are poverty and income inequality. To sidestep is to go around a problem without dealing with it. So the claim is that the measures treat the surface of obesity and leave its causes alone.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) says the measures address the core problems, the opposite of sidestep. (B) reverses the cause: the passage makes poverty and inequality the causes of obesity, not obesity the cause of poverty. (C) repeats the error of (A) and adds a prediction of success that the passage never makes. (D) says the measures address the problem superficially, which is the same claim as sidestepping the core problems.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (D) restates the passage without changing its direction, so the answer is (D).

shortcut.body: Find the verb that carries the author's judgement: sidestep, meaning avoid. Choose the option that expresses avoiding the root cause, here superficially, and cross out the options that say the measures work or reverse the cause. About a minute.

traps.text: It states the opposite of the passage, which says the measures sidestep the core problems. Reading the first sentence alone, where the measures are only proposed, leads here.
It turns the causal arrow around. Poverty and inequality cause obesity in the passage, and a reader who skims to the word obesity may reverse it.
It keeps the wrong half of (A) and adds likely to succeed, a prediction nowhere in the passage. A summary may not add claims.

recognize.clues: The question asks which statement summarizes the passage. A proposal is reported first and then challenged with the verb sidestep, so the author's objection is the point to restate.
recognize.contrast: An inference question accepts any one statement forced by the text. A summary must cover the main claim and keep its direction, so an option that adds a prediction or reverses the cause fails even if it sounds related.

check.body: Deletion test: remove the first sentence and keep only the author's objection. The summary should survive unchanged. The kept option does, while the options that praise the measures, reverse the cause, or predict success each need information the objection does not give.

hints.text: What is the author's own judgement about the measures, as opposed to what the passage only reports about them?
A summary keeps the main claim and its direction, in fewer words.
A good summary adds no claim and reverses no relation. An option that predicts an outcome or flips cause and effect is not a summary.
Find the sentence where the author turns from describing the proposal to judging it, and restate it in your own words. Then compare the direction of each option with yours.
Underline the verb after "Such measures" in the judging sentence and say it in your own words.

variation.stem:
Some people propose that cities cut traffic by adding more lanes to highways. This approach skirts the real cause of congestion: too many people have no good alternative to driving.

Which one of the following statements summarizes the passage?
options: Adding lanes tackles the real cause of congestion and is sure to cut traffic.
If congestion falls, people will gain alternatives to driving, since congestion causes the lack of them.
Adding lanes deals with the symptom of congestion and leaves its cause untouched.
Cities should ban cars from highways to cut congestion.
variation.explanation: The author reports a proposal, then says it skirts the real cause, meaning it avoids it. The summary keeps that judgement: the lanes treat the symptom. One wrong option says the lanes tackle the cause, one reverses cause and effect, and one adds a recommendation the passage never makes.

questions.stem: Raman is confident of speaking English __________ six months as he has been practising regularly __________ the last three weeks.

steps.title: Prepositions of time: what each one needs
steps.body: A preposition of time ties a stretch of time to an event. For + a length (for six months, for three weeks) says how long something lasts or has lasted. Since + a starting point (since Monday, since 2019) names when it began and never takes a length. Within + a length means before that period ends, so it sets a deadline. During + a named period or event (during the war, during the summer) says something happens inside it and does not take a bare count such as six months.

steps.title: Blank 2: has been practising regularly __ the last three weeks
steps.body: Has been practising is the present perfect continuous, an activity that began in the past and runs up to now. The phrase the last three weeks is a length measured back from now, not a starting point, so the word before it is for. Since would need a point such as since last month. That removes (B) and leaves for as the second word of (A) and (D).

steps.title: Blank 1: confident of speaking English __ six months
steps.body: Raman is confident that he will speak English well before six months have gone by. That is a deadline, and the word for a deadline is within. For six months would make him confident of speaking English for a duration of six months, which does not follow from his practice, and during needs a named period. So (D) within, for is the only pair that works in both places.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The pair within, for fits the deadline in the first blank and the duration in the second, which is option (D).

shortcut.body: Do blank 2 first. A length measured back from now with has been practising takes for, which keeps only (A) and (D) and removes (B) and (C), whose second words are since and in. Then blank 1 is a deadline, so within gives (D). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: During six months sounds natural as a span of time, but during belongs with a named period or event. With a bare count of months it does not express the deadline the sentence needs.
It pairs for with since. Since the last three weeks mixes a starting-point word with a length, and since needs a point such as since June.
For six months is the common duration phrase, and in the last three weeks is heard in everyday speech, so the pair reads smoothly. The first blank needs a deadline, which for does not give.

recognize.clues: Two blanks, each before a time phrase. Six months is a length looking ahead to a deadline for a skill, and the last three weeks is a length counted back from now with the continuing verb has been practising.
recognize.contrast: For takes a length and since takes a starting point. Within sets a limit before the period ends, while during goes with a named period or event rather than a bare count.

check.body: Swap test on the filled sentence. Replace within with for: speaking English for six months says how long he will speak, which is not what confidence after practice means. Replace the second for with since: since the last three weeks names no starting point. Both swaps break the sentence.
