hints.text: For each blank, ask what the time phrase measures: a limit by which something happens, a length of time that has run, or a starting point.
Some time prepositions take a length, some take a starting point, and one sets a limit before a period ends.
With a continuing action that has run up to now, measured by a length, one particular preposition fits. A starting-point word cannot take a length.
Settle the second blank first, since it follows has been practising and a length measured back from now. Use that to prune pairs, then fit the first blank.
The word since needs a point in time such as a date, and three weeks is a length. Any pair that ends in since can go.

variation.stem: Meera hopes to finish the course __________ two years, having studied hard __________ last January.
variation.explanation: Last January is a starting point, so the second blank takes since. Finishing the course in two years is a deadline, so the first blank takes within. For needs a length rather than a point, and during needs a named period.

questions.stem: His knowledge of the subject was excellent but his classroom performance was __________.

steps.title: Contrast words and polarity
steps.body: A contrast word such as but, however, although or yet tells the reader that the second part of a sentence opposes the first. Call a word positive if it expresses approval (excellent, good) and negative if it expresses disapproval (poor, weak). After a contrast word the blank must have the opposite polarity from the part before it.

steps.title: Apply it to this sentence
steps.body: The first part says his knowledge was excellent, which is positive. The word but flips direction, so the blank must be negative: his classroom performance fell short of his knowledge.

steps.title: Sort the options by polarity
steps.body: Extremely poor is negative. Good is positive. Desirable is positive, since it means worth wanting. Praiseworthy is positive, since it means deserving praise. Only one option is negative.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The blank needs a negative word, so the answer is extremely poor, option (A).

shortcut.body: Mark the first part positive, read but as a flip, and look for the one negative word. Exactly one option is negative. Twenty seconds. If two options were negative, compare their strength.

traps.text: Good reads well as a description of performance alone, so a reader who ignores the word but accepts it. The sentence needs a contrast, and good agrees with excellent instead.
Desirable can be misread as not yet desirable, which feels like a shortfall. On its own it is a positive word, so it echoes excellent and gives no contrast.
Praiseworthy is positive. It continues the praise of the first half and ignores the contrast that but announces.

recognize.clues: The word but joins excellent knowledge to a blank about classroom performance, and every option is a single evaluative word, so the blank must flip the praise.
recognize.contrast: A sentence joined by and would take a matching positive word. Here but reverses the direction, so a word that agrees with excellent is a lure.

check.body: Read each option back into the sentence and ask whether but still does any work. With any word of praise, the sentence says excellent knowledge but good performance, which contradicts nothing, so the contrast word is wasted. Only one option makes the sentence need but.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2020 GA question 2
GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi (organising institute), print of its paper-and-key web page, IIT Guwahati archive

hints.text: Does the second half of the sentence agree with the first half or push against it? Which word tells you?
Words such as but, however and yet signal contrast, while words such as and and also signal continuation.
After a contrast word, the blank must carry the opposite sense from the first clause. First decide whether that clause is praise or criticism.
Label the first clause positive or negative, flip the label, and then give each option the same kind of label.
The first clause praises his knowledge. Count how many options express disapproval rather than praise.

variation.stem: The plot of the film was gripping but its acting was __________.
variation.explanation: Gripping is praise and but flips the direction, so the blank needs a word of criticism. Wooden means stiff and lifeless. The other three are praise and would leave but without any contrast to mark.

questions.stem:
The dawn of the 21st century witnessed the melting glaciers oscillating between giving too much and too little to billions of people who depend on them for fresh water. The UN climate report estimates that without deep cuts to man-made emissions, at least 30% of the northern hemisphere’s surface permafrost could melt by the end of the century. Given this situation of imminent global exodus of billions of people displaced by rising seas, nation-states need to rethink their carbon footprint for political concerns, if not for environmental ones.

Which one of the following statements can be inferred from the given passage?
options: Nation-states do not have environmental concerns.
Nation-states are responsible for providing fresh water to billions of people.
Billions of people are responsible for man-made emissions.
Billions of people are affected by melting glaciers.

steps.title: What can be inferred
steps.body: An inference must follow from what the passage states, with no help from outside knowledge. A statement the passage only hints at, or a plausible-sounding extra claim, is not an inference. For each option ask: which sentence of the passage makes this true?

steps.title: List what the passage actually says
steps.body: Glaciers deliver too much or too little water to billions of people who depend on them for fresh water. Without cuts in emissions, much permafrost could melt. Rising seas could displace billions of people. Nation-states should rethink their carbon footprint for political reasons, if not for environmental ones.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) The phrase if not for environmental ones suggests environmental concern may be weak, but the passage never says states have none. (B) The passage says people depend on glaciers for water, not that states are responsible for supplying it. (C) The passage says nothing about who causes the emissions. (D) Billions of people depend on the melting glaciers and are exposed to displacement, so billions are affected, which the first and third sentences state.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (D) is stated by the passage, so the answer is (D).

shortcut.body: Hunt for the option that repeats a fact from the passage in other words. Billions of people appears twice, tied to glaciers and to displacement, and only (D) uses it that way. Strike the options that blame or assign duties. About a minute.

traps.text: It stretches a hint, if not for environmental ones, into a flat claim that states have no environmental concern. The passage implies at most that political reasons are a safer appeal.
It confuses depend on with are responsible for. People depend on glaciers for fresh water, and the passage names no supplier.
It adds a cause that the passage never gives. The passage mentions billions of people as affected, and a reader who links billions with emissions is importing blame.

recognize.clues: The question asks what can be inferred, and the options reuse passage words (billions of people, fresh water, emissions, nation-states) while changing the relation between them.
recognize.contrast: A main-idea question asks for the gist of the passage. Here one narrow statement only has to be supported, so a claim that is true to the passage but small can be the answer.

check.body: Negation test: suppose the kept option were false. Then the opening sentences about billions depending on the glaciers and facing displacement would lose their meaning. Negating each of the other three leaves the passage intact, so none of them is forced by it.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2020 GA question 4

hints.text: For each option, which sentence of the passage would you point to as proof? If there is none, it is not an inference.
An inference is a statement the passage supports on its own, not a guess about what the author might think.
Watch for options that change a relation between the passage's words, or turn a hint into a flat claim.
List who the passage says is affected, what it says causes the problem, and what it asks nation-states to do. Compare each option against that list.
Compare each option with your list, and drop any that adds a cause or a duty the passage does not state.

variation.stem:
Over the last decade the river delta has lost nearly a fifth of its mangrove cover. Millions of fishing families rely on the mangroves as nurseries for fish. Officials warn that without protection, storm surges will reach inland villages, and urge the state to treat mangrove loss as a livelihood matter, if not as a conservation one.

Which one of the following statements can be inferred from the given passage?
options: The state is responsible for planting every mangrove.
Fishing families caused the loss of mangroves.
Many families depend on the mangroves for a living.
Officials have no interest in conservation.
variation.explanation: The second sentence says millions of fishing families rely on the mangroves, which supports the statement directly. The other three add duties, blame or a flat denial that the passage never states; the phrase if not as a conservation one only hints at a priority.

questions.stem:
Goods and Services Tax (GST) is an indirect tax introduced in India in 2017 that is imposed on the supply of goods and services, and it subsumes all indirect taxes except few. It is a destination-based tax imposed on goods and services used, and it is not imposed at the point of origin from where goods come. GST also has a few components specific to state governments, central government and Union Territories (UTs).

Which one of the following statements can be inferred from the given passage?
options: GST is imposed on the production of goods and services.
GST does not have a component specific to UT.
GST is imposed at the point of usage of goods and services.

steps.title: Inference by checking each claim against the text
steps.body: An inference must be forced by the passage. The quickest test is to find the sentence that supports an option, and to look for words in the option that the passage contradicts. A destination-based tax is charged where the goods are used or consumed, not where they are made.

steps.title: Facts in the passage
steps.body: GST is charged on the supply of goods and services. It subsumes all indirect taxes except a few. It is destination-based, imposed on goods and services used, and not at the point of origin. It has a few components specific to states, the centre and UTs.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) says it is imposed on production, but the passage says not at the point of origin. (B) says all indirect taxes, but the passage says all except few. (C) says no UT component, but the passage lists UTs among the bodies with specific components. (D) imposed at the point of usage is the same as destination-based, imposed on goods and services used.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Options (A), (B) and (C) each contradict a sentence of the passage, and (D) restates one, so the answer is (D).

shortcut.body: Three options contradict the passage in one word each: production, all, no. Option (D) is the destination-based sentence in other words. About a minute.

traps.text: It names the opposite end of the chain. The passage says the tax is not imposed at the point of origin, where goods are produced.
It drops the words except few. The passage says GST takes in all indirect taxes except a few, so it does not include all of them.
It denies what the last sentence says. The passage lists Union Territories among the bodies that have components specific to them.

recognize.clues: A definition-style passage, and options that swap the passage's careful words for absolute ones: all in place of except few, no in place of a named component, production in place of usage.
recognize.contrast: A summary question asks for the overall point of the passage. An inference question only needs one statement supported by a specific sentence, so you test the options one at a time.

check.body: Quote check: each of three options has a phrase in the passage that denies it (not at the point of origin, except few, the list that includes UTs). The remaining option has a phrase that confirms it (goods and services used). Three denials and one confirmation agree.

GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi (organising institute), print of its paper-and-key web page, IIT Guwahati archive

hints.text: Which words in each option are absolute, such as all, no, or a place in the chain like production, and does the passage allow them?
In an inference question, each option needs one sentence of the passage that backs it.
An option that contradicts any one sentence of the passage cannot be an inference. Test each option against the sentence that covers its topic.
Note three facts: how much of the indirect tax system GST covers, where it is imposed, and which bodies have specific components. Then check each option against them.
The passage says GST covers all indirect taxes except a few, and it names the bodies with specific components. Two options clash with those sentences directly.

variation.stem:
The Municipal Entry Fee is a levy collected by the city on vehicles that enter the old town. It replaces the earlier parking and toll charges except for the bridge toll. It is charged on entry, not on registration of the vehicle. Vehicles registered inside the old town get a monthly pass in place of the per-entry fee.

Which one of the following statements can be inferred from the given passage?
options: The fee replaces every earlier charge.
The fee is charged when a vehicle enters the old town.
The fee is charged when a vehicle is registered.
Vehicles registered inside the old town pay the per-entry fee like all others.
variation.explanation: The passage says the fee is charged on entry, which is the second option. Every earlier charge ignores the bridge toll, registration is stated as not the trigger, and local vehicles get a monthly pass instead of the per-entry fee.

questions.stem: The expenditure on the project _____ as follows: equipment Rs.20 lakhs, salaries Rs.12 lakhs, and contingency Rs.3 lakhs.

steps.title: Two things decide the blank
steps.body: First, agreement: in the present tense the verb takes -s when its subject is singular (it breaks) and no -s when the subject is plural (they break). The subject is the head noun of the subject phrase. Words after a preposition such as on belong to a modifier and do not change the head. Second, meaning: break down is a phrasal verb that means to be divided into parts or categories, which is what a cost does when it is itemised. Break alone means to snap or to stop working.

steps.title: Find the subject and its number
steps.body: Strip the modifier on the project. What is left is the expenditure, a singular noun. The three items after the colon are the contents of the list, not part of the subject. The verb must therefore be breaks, not break. This removes (A) and (B).

steps.title: Choose between breaks down and breaks
steps.body: The sentence introduces an itemised list with as follows, so the verb has to say that the total is divided into those parts: the expenditure breaks down as follows. The bare verb breaks would say the expenditure snaps, which makes no sense here. This removes (D).

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The singular verb with the dividing sense is breaks down, option (C).

shortcut.body: Two filters. A singular subject, expenditure, removes (A) and (B). The itemised list after as follows needs break down, which removes (D). Thirty seconds.

traps.text: The three listed items make the subject feel plural, so a reader picks break down. The list is the content, and the subject is the single noun expenditure.
It is plural and it uses break in the sense of snap. It fails the agreement test and the meaning test.
It agrees correctly with the singular subject but misses the phrasal verb. Breaks alone does not mean divide into categories, so the sentence reads as if the cost snapped.

recognize.clues: A long subject (the expenditure on the project), a colon introducing a list of three items, and options that differ in the -s ending and in the particle down.
recognize.contrast: The three listed amounts look plural but are the contents of the list, not the subject, so agreement follows expenditure. Break versus break down is a separate check on meaning, not on number.

check.body: Synonym test: the expenditure is divided as follows is correct English, and break down is the phrasal verb with that meaning, in the singular form. By contrast, the expenditure breaks as follows would mean the expenditure snaps, which no reader intends.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2019 GA question 1
GATE 2019 CS final answer key (organised by IIT Madras), gateexam.info copy

hints.text: Cover the phrase that starts with on. What is the subject of the verb, and what does the sentence do with the list after the colon?
A present-tense verb takes -s with a singular subject. A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word that together carry one meaning.
Words inside a modifying phrase do not decide agreement; only the head noun does. The meaning must also fit: does the verb explain how a total is divided into items?
First filter the options by number to see which remain. Then read the remaining ones into the sentence and ask which describes splitting a total into parts.
The head noun is singular, so the two options without the -s ending can go.

variation.stem: The cost of the repairs _____ as follows: paint Rs.8 thousand, wiring Rs.5 thousand and plumbing Rs.4 thousand.
variation.explanation: The head noun is cost, which is singular, so the verb takes -s; the plural word repairs belongs to a modifier. The cost is then divided into itemised parts, which is the meaning of break down. Breaks alone means snaps, and the forms without -s disagree with cost.

questions.stem: The search engine’s business model ___________ around the fulcrum of trust.

steps.title: How a fill in the blank is decided
steps.body: The missing word has to fit three things. It must fit the grammar of the slot, it must pair naturally with the words next to it (a collocation), and it must fit the picture the sentence draws. A fulcrum is the point on which a lever turns or balances, so the sentence pictures something turning about a central support.

steps.title: Grammar and pairing
steps.body: The subject is the singular noun model, so the verb needs the -s form, and all four options have it. Grammar therefore does not separate them. The words around the blank do: the verb is followed by around, and the fixed phrase is revolve around, meaning have something as the centre on which everything turns.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) revolves around: the business model has trust as its centre, which matches the fulcrum image. (B) plays around means to fool about, which says nothing about a central support. (C) sinks takes into or under, not around the fulcrum. (D) bursts takes into or out, and a model that explodes is not a statement about trust.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The only verb that pairs with around and with a fulcrum is revolves, option (A).

shortcut.body: Read the verb with around and fulcrum together. Revolve around a pivot is a stock pairing, so the answer comes in about fifteen seconds. Unsafe only when two options both collocate with around.

traps.text: Plays around is a real phrase, so it sounds familiar next to around. It means to mess about, and the sentence is about a central support.
Sinks suggests a business model in trouble. The sentence talks about a pivot, and sinks does not combine with around.
Bursts is a vivid verb that a reader might pick because search engines grow fast, but it pairs with into or out and not with around a fulcrum.

recognize.clues: The word right after the blank (around) and the noun fulcrum, which supplies a picture of something turning about a central support.
recognize.contrast: Grammar clues cannot split the options here, since all four are singular verbs. This differs from a tense or agreement item, where the verb form itself decides.

check.body: Substitute the chosen verb back and read the whole sentence: the model turns about trust as its centre, and the phrase is a stock pairing. Replace it with each other verb and each one loses either the pairing with around or the pivot picture.

Choose the verb whose usual partner is the next word and whose picture matches the noun at the end. A fulcrum is a pivot point.

Two options are about falling or breaking, and neither pairs with around in this way. Compare the remaining two on the pivot picture.

Plays around and hangs around are real phrases but mean fooling about and loitering, and sinks does not mean having it as the centre.

questions.stem:
“A recent High Court judgement has sought to dispel the idea of begging as a disease — which leads to its stigmatization and criminalization — and to regard it as a symptom. The underlying disease is the failure of the state to protect citizens who fall through the social security net.”

Which one of the following statements can be inferred from the given passage?
options: Beggars are lazy people who beg because they are unwilling to work
Beggars are created because of the lack of social welfare schemes
Begging is an offence that has to be dealt with firmly
Begging has to be banned because it adversely affects the welfare of the state

steps.title: Disease and symptom
steps.body: A disease is a cause, and a symptom is a visible sign of a cause that lies elsewhere. Treating begging as a disease places the fault in the beggar, which the passage says leads to stigma and criminalisation. Treating it as a symptom places the cause somewhere else. An inference must follow the reframing the author reports, not the view the author sets aside.

steps.title: What the passage claims
steps.body: The judgement seeks to dispel the idea of begging as a disease and to regard it as a symptom. The underlying disease is the failure of the state to protect citizens who fall through the social security net. So people beg because the state's protection failed to reach them.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) blames the beggar for laziness, which is the individual-fault view the judgement rejects. (C) says begging is an offence to be dealt with firmly, which is the criminalisation the passage questions. (D) says it should be banned, which is the same view in stronger form. (B) says beggars arise from the lack of social welfare, and failure of the state to protect citizens who fall through the net means exactly that welfare did not reach them.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only (B) follows the passage, so the answer is (B).

shortcut.body: Three options blame or punish the beggar, which the passage argues against. Only (B) puts the cause in the state's welfare failure. About a minute.

traps.text: It repeats the stigma the judgement wants to dispel. Nothing in the passage says beggars are lazy or unwilling to work.
It reads like the legal conclusion of a passage about a court, but the court is moving away from criminalisation, so firm action is the view being set aside.
A ban is the criminalising response the passage criticises, and the passage never says begging harms the state.

recognize.clues: A short passage that reports a court rejecting one framing (disease) for another (symptom), with options that revive the rejected framing in stronger words.
recognize.contrast: A main-idea question asks for the passage as a whole. Here a single claim must follow from the stated reason, so each option is tested against the passage line by line.

check.body: Second route: restate the passage as a question of who is at fault, and the passage places the fault with the state and not with the person who begs. Ask of each option whom it holds at fault or what it would do to that person, and compare.

hints.text: Whose view does the passage set aside, and whose view does it adopt?
An inference is a statement the passage supports without adding new facts or opinions.

Write one line for what the old view blamed and one line for what the passage names as the underlying fault. Then test each option against those two lines.

questions.stem:
“From where are they bringing their books? ________ bringing _______ books from _____.”

The words that best fill the blanks in the above sentence are

steps.title: Three words that sound the same
steps.body: Their means belonging to them and comes before a noun: their books. They're is the contraction of they are and must be followed by a verb form such as bringing. There names a place: over there, from there. A test for each: if you can say they are in its place, write they're; if you can say belonging to them, write their; if you can say that place, write there.

steps.title: Blank 1: ___ bringing
steps.body: The slot needs a subject and a helping verb before bringing, so it reads They are bringing. The word is They're.

steps.title: Blank 2 and blank 3
steps.body: Blank 2 comes before the noun books and shows ownership, so it is their. Blank 3 follows from and refers to the place the books are coming from, so it is there. The sentence reads: They're bringing their books from there.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The order They're, their, there is option (B).

shortcut.body: Fill the middle blank first. A word before the noun books that shows ownership is their, and only (B) and (C) have their there. Blank 1 then needs they are, so (B). Fifteen seconds.

traps.text: It begins with Their, which is a possessive and cannot take the place of they are before bringing. It also puts they're where the ownership word belongs.
It starts with There, which names a place and cannot be the subject of bringing. It also ends with they're, which cannot follow from.
It uses there for the ownership slot because their and there sound the same. The middle blank needs their before books.

recognize.clues: Three blanks filled by the same trio of homophones, each with a different neighbour: a verb form, a noun, and the preposition from.
recognize.contrast: Spelling confusions of this kind are decided by the word each blank sits beside. A vocabulary item decides by meaning of the whole sentence instead.

check.body: Read the filled sentence with the first blank expanded to they are and the second replaced by belonging to them. If both substitutions keep the sense and the last blank can be replaced by that place, the filling is consistent. A different filling breaks at least one substitution.

hints.text: The three blanks take the same three look-alike words. What differs in how each blank is used?
Three words sound alike: one shows ownership, one is a contraction of two words, and one names a place.
Expand a contraction to test it. If the blank reads naturally as they are, the contraction fits. If the next word is a noun owned by someone, use the possessive.
Take each blank in turn and ask what comes next: a verb form, a noun, or nothing at all after from.
Expand the first blank into two words and see whether the sentence still reads naturally.

variation.stem: Are the guests here? ________ waiting for ________ friends near the gate, but ________ is no sign of them.
variation.explanation: The first blank needs they are before waiting, so they’re. The second comes before the noun friends and shows ownership, so their. The third begins a statement that something is absent, so there. Each other option fails at least one of these substitutions.

questions.stem:
“A _________ investigation can sometimes yield new facts, but typically organized ones are more successful.”

The word that best fills the blank in the above sentence is

steps.title: Read the contrast and its anchor
steps.body: The word but marks a contrast, and the pronoun ones points back to investigations: some investigations versus organized ones. The blank therefore describes investigations of a kind that is the opposite of organized. Rule: find the anchor word on the far side of the contrast, here organized, and choose the option that is its opposite in meaning.

steps.title: Test each option against organized
steps.body: Meandering means wandering without a fixed course, which is the opposite of organized. Timely means on time, which has nothing to do with organization. Consistent means steady and uniform, which is close to organized and not opposite. Systematic means done by a method, which is a synonym of organized.

steps.title: Check the meaning in the sentence
steps.body: A meandering investigation can sometimes yield new facts, but organized ones are more successful reads sensibly: a loose search sometimes stumbles on something, but a planned one usually does better. With systematic, the sentence would say that systematic investigations yield facts but organized ones do better, which sets two similar things against each other.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The opposite of organized is meandering, option (A).

shortcut.body: Circle organized ones after the but and ask which option means the opposite. Systematic is its synonym and is the planted lure. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: Timely is a pleasant word that often goes with investigation, but it describes timing, not organisation, so it creates no contrast with organized.
Consistent sounds methodical and close to organized, which makes it the wrong direction for a contrast.
Systematic is the most natural partner of investigation, so it attracts readers who skip the but. It means organized, which the sentence needs the blank to oppose.

recognize.clues: The contrast word but, and the pronoun ones, which points back to investigations and sets organized ones against the blank.
recognize.contrast: A plain vocabulary item asks which word fits the meaning. Here the contrast signal fixes the direction, so the blank must oppose organized rather than match it.

check.body: Replace the blank with the opposite of organized, then with a synonym of organized. With the synonym the sentence sets two similar things against each other and the but loses its job. With the opposite the contrast reads naturally, so the first choice holds.

hints.text: What does the word but tell you about how the two halves of the sentence relate?
A contrast word sets two things against each other, so the blank must describe the opposite of whatever it is contrasted with.
Find the anchor on the other side of the contrast and choose the option whose meaning is opposite to it, not close to it.
Underline the word describing the investigations after but. Then mark each option as same direction, opposite direction, or unrelated.
Two options are near-synonyms of the anchor, and one has nothing to do with organisation. Only one option names the opposite of being organised.

variation.stem: A ____________ reading of the report may catch a few errors, but a careful, line-by-line one is far more reliable.
variation.explanation: The word but sets the blank against careful, line-by-line reading, so the blank must mean the opposite: quick and shallow, which is cursory. Thorough, meticulous and painstaking all agree in direction with the anchor, so they would remove the contrast.

questions.stem: Choose the option with words that are not synonyms.

steps.title: Synonyms and the odd pair
steps.body: Synonyms are words that mean nearly the same thing in the same sense. The question asks for the one pair whose words are not synonyms. Test a pair by asking whether one word could stand in for the other in a sentence without changing the meaning.

steps.title: Check each pair
steps.body: Aversion is a strong dislike, so aversion and dislike are synonyms. Luminous means giving off light and radiant means shining brightly, so they are synonyms. Plunder means to rob by force and loot means to steal in a disorderly way, so they are synonyms. Yielding means giving way or soft, and resistant means pushing back or withstanding. These point in opposite directions.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Only yielding and resistant fail the test, so the answer is (D).

shortcut.body: Read each pair and ask whether you could swap the words. Three swap, and yielding and resistant do not. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: Aversion is stronger than dislike, so a reader who notices the difference in degree thinks the pair differs. They still point the same way, so they are synonyms.
Luminous is about giving light and radiant about shining out. The two senses are close enough that dictionaries list them as synonyms.
Plunder and loot both mean to take goods by force, usually in war or riot, so they are synonyms even though one is more formal.

recognize.clues: The instruction to choose words that are not synonyms, which turns the usual hunt for a matching pair into a hunt for the one pair that fails.
recognize.contrast: An analogy item asks for a relation between pairs. This item compares the two words inside each pair only.

check.body: Second route: find an opposite of one word in each pair and see which pair holds it. The opposite of yielding is unbending, and resistant describes exactly that, so that pair holds opposites. For the other three pairs, no opposite of the first word describes its partner.

hints.text: The question asks for the pair that fails a test. What is the test for two words being synonyms?
Synonyms point the same way in meaning and can usually replace each other in a sentence.
A pair that points in opposite directions, even if both words are about the same topic, is not a pair of synonyms.
For each pair, write a short sentence with the first word, then swap in the second and see whether the meaning holds.
Three pairs survive the swap with only a small change of strength or formality. One pair reverses the meaning when swapped.

questions.stem: Saturn is __________ to be seen on a clear night with the naked eye.

steps.title: Where enough goes
steps.body: Enough means to the degree that is needed. Its place depends on the word it goes with. With an adjective or an adverb it comes after the word: bright enough, fast enough, clearly enough. With a noun it comes before the noun: enough water. When it is followed by to and a verb, the pattern is adjective + enough + to + verb.

steps.title: Apply the pattern
steps.body: The slot is followed by to be seen, so the pattern is adjective + enough + to + verb. The adjective is bright, so the filled phrase is bright enough to be seen.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) enough bright puts enough before an adjective, which is wrong. (B) bright enough has the right order. (C) as enough bright adds an as that no pattern allows. (D) bright as enough splits the pattern and has no meaning.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The correct order is bright enough, option (B).

shortcut.body: Enough goes after an adjective: bright enough. Ten seconds. Safe whenever enough modifies an adjective or adverb, as bright does here. If it modifies a noun it goes before it (enough light), so check which word it modifies first.

traps.text: It puts enough in front of bright, which is where it goes before a noun (enough light). Before an adjective it must come after.
It mixes the as ... as frame with enough, which never combine. It reads like an equal comparison and has no meaning here.
It places as before enough, as if enough were an adjective in an as ... as frame. Enough is not used this way.

recognize.clues: The word enough in every option, the adjective bright, and the infinitive to be seen after the blank.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with the as ... as comparison frame. Enough marks a sufficient degree and does not take as.

check.body: Test the chosen order with a second adjective: fast enough to catch the bus, tall enough to reach the shelf. Both put enough after the adjective, the same order as the answer. The reverse order is correct only with a noun, as in enough time.

hints.text: Does the word enough describe an adjective, an adverb, or a noun here?
The position of enough depends on the word it describes.
Before a noun, enough comes first. After an adjective or an adverb, it comes second.
The sentence ends with to be seen, so the slot holds a description of Saturn followed by enough. Identify which word is the description.
The adjective here is bright. Now check which options put enough before it and which put it after, and drop any that add an extra word.

variation.stem: The tea is ________ to drink without waiting.
variation.explanation: The word described is the adjective cool, so enough comes after it and is followed by to and a verb. Putting enough before an adjective is wrong, and as cannot join the pattern.

questions.stem:
“We lived in a culture that denied any merit to literary works, considering them important only when they were handmaidens to something seemingly more urgent – namely ideology. This was a country where all gestures, even the most private, were interpreted in political terms.”

The author’s belief that ideology is not as important as literature is revealed by the word:

steps.title: Words that reveal the author's own view
steps.body: A hedge is a word that marks a statement as an appearance or as someone else's impression, so the author does not commit to it. Examples are seemingly, apparently, supposedly and allegedly. When a question asks which word reveals the author's belief, look for the hedge, because it separates the author's view from the view being described.

steps.title: Whose view is in the sentence
steps.body: The sentence describes a culture that valued literary works only when they served something more urgent, namely ideology. That is the culture's view. The author does not say that ideology is more urgent. The word seemingly places the urgency in doubt: it only appears more urgent. So the author does not accept that ideology outranks literature.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Culture names the society and carries no judgement. Urgent states what the culture believed, so it reports their view. Political describes how gestures were interpreted. Only seemingly shows the author stepping back from the claim.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The word is seemingly, option (B).

shortcut.body: Scan for a hedge adverb such as seemingly, apparently or supposedly. It is the word where the author steps away from the claim. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: Culture is the subject the author criticises, and it names the setting. It does not mark the author's opinion about ideology.
Urgent states what the culture believed, so it is part of the view the author is reporting. The author hedges it with seemingly.
Political describes how the culture read private gestures. It supports the author's complaint about ideology but does not show the author's ranking of ideology and literature.

recognize.clues: The question asks which single word reveals the author’s belief, while the sentence reports the culture’s view of ideology as more pressing.
recognize.contrast: A question on the main idea needs the passage as a whole. This one is solved at word level by spotting a hedge that separates the author from the reported view.

check.body: Delete each option in turn and re-read. Removing the hedge makes the author assert that ideology really is more urgent, which reverses the stated belief. Removing any of the other three words changes the description but leaves the author’s stance untouched, so only one word is load-bearing for the belief.

hints.text: Which word in the sentence tells you the author is not simply agreeing with the culture being described?
Some words show distance from a claim: they mark it as an appearance or as someone else’s impression.
To find an author’s own belief, separate the view being reported from the words that cast doubt on it.
Split the sentence into what the culture said and what the author adds, then ask where each option falls.

variation.explanation: Supposedly marks the generosity as an appearance, so the author does not accept it. Scheme and harvest are plain nouns, and price states a fact about the terms without showing the author’s doubt.

questions.stem: After Rajendra Chola returned from his voyage to Indonesia, he ______ to visit the temple in Thanjavur.

steps.title: Order of events and past tenses
steps.body: The simple past (returned, wished) reports an event at a past time. The past perfect (had + past participle) marks an event that happened before another past event. A past narrative therefore uses the simple past for events in the order they happened, and reserves the past perfect for an event that came earlier than the one it is compared with. The word after already says which event is first, so the later event needs no special form.

steps.title: Put the two events on a time line
steps.body: Event 1 is that he returned from Indonesia. Event 2 is the wishing to visit the temple. The word After says that event 2 follows event 1, so the wishing is the later event, and the later event stays in the simple past: he wished.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) was wishing is a progressive form of a verb of wanting, which is awkward and suggests an activity in progress. (B) is wishing is present tense and clashes with the past narrative. (D) had wished places the wishing before the return, which contradicts After. (C) wished fits.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The sentence needs the simple past for the later event, option (C).

shortcut.body: Mark the order. After X, Y: Y comes later, so Y takes the simple past. Present forms do not belong in a past story. Thirty seconds.

traps.text: Was wishing makes a state of wanting into a progressive action. The sentence reports a wish that arose, so the simple past fits.
Is wishing is present tense. The sentence tells a past story, so present forms clash with returned.

After suggests an earlier event, and a reader reaches for the past perfect. But the clause after After holds the earlier event, and the wishing is the later one, so the perfect would reverse the order.

recognize.clues: The word After at the start, the past tense returned in the first clause, and options that mix past, present and perfect forms.
recognize.contrast: Past perfect is for the earlier of two past events. Because the blank is the later event here, the plain past is the contrast to the perfect form.

check.body: Second route: ask whether the wish is a single event that arises or an activity going on over a stretch of time. A wish that comes up after a voyage is a single event, which separates the plain past from the progressive. The present form is ruled out by the past narrative, and the perfect form by placing the wish before the return.

hints.text: Which event happened first, the return or the wish, and which word in the sentence tells you?
Simple past reports an event at a past time. Past perfect marks an event before another past event.
The perfect form is for the earlier of two past events.
Write the two events in order and note which one the sentence says came first.
Place the two events on a line in the order the sentence gives them, and mark which of the two the blank describes.

variation.stem: After the river flooded the village, the headman ______ to move the market uphill.
variation.explanation: After puts the flood first, so the decision is the later event and takes the simple past. Had decided would put the decision before the flood, and is deciding is present tense. Was deciding turns a single decision into an action in progress.

questions.stem: Research in the workplace reveals that people work for many reasons __________.

steps.title: Beside and besides
steps.body: Beside is a preposition of position and means next to: sit beside me. Besides means in addition to or apart from: besides money, besides his salary. Besides can also be an adverb meaning also, as in He is rich; besides, he is kind. A preposition comes before its object, so besides money has the right order and money besides does not.

steps.title: What the sentence says
steps.body: People work for many reasons, and money is one of them. The blank adds other reasons on top of money, so it means in addition to money. The word is besides, placed before its object money.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) money beside has the object before the preposition and means next to. (B) beside money keeps the order but means next to money, which has no sense here. (C) money besides puts the object first, which a preposition does not allow. (D) besides money has the right word in the right order.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The phrase is besides money, option (D).

shortcut.body: Substitute in addition to. Besides money becomes in addition to money, and only (D) keeps the order a preposition needs. Twenty seconds.

traps.text: It combines the wrong word with the wrong order. Beside means next to, and money would have to come after the preposition.
The order is right, but beside means next to. People do not work for reasons next to money.
It has the right word, besides, but the object comes first. A preposition comes before its object, so money besides is not a phrase.

recognize.clues: The options pair the same two words, beside and besides, in both orders, and the blank follows a sentence about many reasons people work.
recognize.contrast: The articles-and-prepositions topic covers choosing a preposition for a fixed phrase. Here the choice turns on the meaning of two near-identical forms plus word order, so test meaning first, then order.

check.body: Run a second route on the finished sentence: "People work for many reasons next to money" reads as a place, not a reason, so beside fails on meaning even when the order is right. Reading the sentence aloud with besides money, it adds money to the list of reasons, which is what the sentence needs.

hints.text: Ask what the blank adds to money: a position next to it, or more reasons on top of it?
Two look-alike words differ in meaning: one is about where something stands, the other is about adding to what was already named.
A preposition sits before the noun it governs, so the word that ties to the noun must come first in the phrase.
Read the sentence with a plain replacement such as "in addition to" and see which word and order survive in each option.
Two options place the noun before the linking word, and that order does not work for a preposition, so they can be set aside first.

variation.stem: Surveys show that employees stay in a job for many reasons __________.
variation.explanation: The blank must mean in addition to pay, so the word is besides, not beside, which means next to. A preposition comes before its object, so besides pay is right and pay besides is not a phrase.

questions.stem:
“The hold of the nationalist imagination on our colonial past is such that anything inadequately or improperly nationalist is just not history.”

Which of the following statements best reflects the author’s opinion?
options: History is viewed through the filter of nationalism.
Nationalism has to be both adequately and properly imagined.

steps.title: Restate, then match direction
steps.body: For a question on the author's opinion, restate the sentence in plain words, then pick the option that keeps both its claim and its direction. The author is describing a pattern (the hold of ... is such that), not recommending it, so an option that recommends or exaggerates changes the claim.

steps.title: Plain restatement
steps.body: The nationalist way of imagining the colonial past has such control over it that anything not nationalist enough, whether inadequately or improperly, is not accepted as history. In other words, only the nationalist version passes as history. The past is seen through a nationalist filter.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (A) plays on the word imagination and says nationalists are creative, which is not about how the past is viewed. (C) is an exaggeration: the sentence says non-nationalist accounts are not counted as history, not that the past did not happen. (D) turns the description into advice. (B) says history is viewed through a nationalist filter, which is the restatement.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The option that matches the restatement is (B).

shortcut.body: Rewrite the sentence in six words: only nationalist accounts count as history. Match (B). Strike options that exaggerate (never happened) or that advise (has to be). About a minute.

traps.text: It picks up the word imagination and builds a claim about nationalists being creative. The sentence is about how the past is seen.
It stretches the claim to the extreme. The sentence says non-nationalist accounts are not counted as history, and that is far from saying the past never happened.
It turns a description of how history is treated into a demand for how nationalism should be imagined. The author reports a pattern and does not prescribe.

recognize.clues: A single dense sentence followed by "best reflects the author's opinion", with options that pick up the word imagination, exaggerate, or turn the description into advice.
recognize.contrast: The rc-method topic is about reading a whole passage for its structure. Here one sentence carries everything, so the skill is restating it and rejecting options that stretch it.

check.body: Second route, a paraphrase test: imagine the author reading each option and asking whether it needs any claim the sentence does not make. (B) needs none, since it only says history is seen through a nationalist lens. (C) needs a claim about events not happening, (D) needs a claim about what nationalism should do, and (A) needs a claim about nationalists being creative. The sentence makes none of these.

hints.text: What is the sentence telling you about the way the past is treated, and is the author describing it or recommending it?
An opinion question asks for the claim the author actually makes, so restate the sentence in plain words before you look at the options.
A faithful option keeps both the content and the direction of the claim. One that exaggerates, advises, or plays on a single word changes it.
Compress the sentence to a short rule: what must an account be to count as history? Then test each option against that rule.

variation.stem:
"Our textbooks treat the dynasty so reverently that any account not praising it is dismissed as gossip, not scholarship."

Which of the following statements best reflects the author's opinion?
options: The dynasty deserved the praise it received.
Scholarship is judged through the filter of dynastic praise.
Gossip has to be both accurate and well written.
variation.explanation: Restate the sentence: only accounts that praise the dynasty count as scholarship. The second option keeps that claim. The first judges the dynasty, the third exaggerates, and the fourth turns a description into advice.
